title: Substantive Testing - Analytical Procedures and Tests of Details
learning_objectives: Understand the nature and purpose of substantive procedures
Distinguish between substantive analytical procedures and tests of details
Know when substantive procedures are required regardless of control reliance
Learn how to design substantive procedures responsive to assessed risks
Understand the effectiveness and limitations of analytical procedures
Apply tests of details to various account balances and assertions
Know how to combine substantive procedures for sufficient appropriate evidence
Understand the relationship between detection risk and extent of substantive testing

content.overview: Substantive procedures are audit procedures designed to detect material misstatements at the assertion level. Unlike tests of controls which evaluate whether controls prevent or detect misstatements, substantive procedures directly test whether misstatements exist in account balances, transactions, or disclosures. AU-C 330 and AS 2301 (PCAOB) require substantive procedures for all relevant assertions related to material account balances, classes of transactions, and disclosures, regardless of the assessed level of control risk. This makes substantive testing a mandatory component of every financial statement audit. Substantive procedures consist of two types: (1) substantive analytical procedures, and (2) tests of details of transactions, balances, and disclosures. The nature, timing, and extent of substantive procedures are determined by the auditor's assessment of risk of material misstatement and desired level of detection risk.

definition_and_purpose.substantive_procedures_definition: Audit procedures performed to detect material misstatements at the assertion level, including tests of details and substantive analytical procedures
primary_purposes: Obtain evidence about the accuracy of amounts and disclosures in financial statements
Detect material misstatements in account balances, transaction classes, and disclosures
Provide direct evidence about financial statement assertions
Reduce detection risk to an acceptable level
Compensate for assessed risks of material misstatement from inherent and control risk

tests_of_controls.focus: How well controls prevent or detect misstatements
tests_of_controls.when_performed: Optional (except in integrated audits) - only when auditor plans to rely on controls
tests_of_controls.impact: Affects assessed control risk and extent of substantive procedures needed

substantive_procedures.evidence_obtained: Direct evidence about account balances and assertions
substantive_procedures.when_performed: Required for all relevant assertions for material accounts
substantive_procedures.impact: Directly reduces detection risk and provides basis for audit opinion

contrast_with_tests_of_controls.key_distinction: Tests of controls ask 'Are controls working?' while substantive procedures ask 'Are the numbers correct?'

requirement_for_substantive_procedures.mandatory_nature: Auditing standards REQUIRE substantive procedures for all relevant assertions related to material classes of transactions, account balances, and disclosures
cannot_be_eliminated: Even when controls are assessed as highly effective, substantive procedures are still required
Controls have inherent limitations (management override, collusion, human error)
Cannot rely solely on controls to detect all material misstatements
Minimum level of substantive testing always required

extent_may_be_reduced.when: Control risk is assessed as low based on effective tests of controls
extent_may_be_reduced.how_much: Professional judgment - depends on control effectiveness and risk assessment
extent_may_be_reduced.minimum: At minimum, substantive analytical procedures or limited tests of details still required
extent_may_be_reduced.example: If controls over revenue are highly effective and tested, may reduce confirmation sample from 80% to 40% of receivables, but cannot eliminate confirmations entirely

specific_requirements.significant_risks: For assertions with significant risk, tests of details are REQUIRED; cannot rely solely on substantive analytical procedures
specific_requirements.cash_and_equivalents: Professional standards specifically require tests of details for cash at period end (bank confirmations)
specific_requirements.material_accounts: All material account balances require some substantive procedures
specific_requirements.related_party_transactions: Require specific substantive procedures due to higher risk

substantive_analytical_procedures.definition: Evaluations of financial information through analysis of plausible relationships among both financial and non-financial data
substantive_analytical_procedures.nature: Indirect evidence obtained by comparing recorded amounts to expected values

tests_of_details.definition: Procedures to obtain direct evidence about specific transactions, account balances, or disclosures
tests_of_details.also_known_as: Detailed testing, substantive tests of transactions/balances
tests_of_details.nature: Direct evidence obtained by examining source documents, confirmations, physical inspection, etc.

substantive_analytical_procedures.description: Use of comparisons and relationships to assess whether account balances and transactions appear reasonable

basic_process: Develop an expectation of what the account balance or ratio should be
Compare recorded amount to expected amount
Investigate significant differences (variances beyond acceptable threshold)
Obtain corroborating evidence for unusual variances
Draw conclusion about whether recorded amount is fairly stated
how_they_work.effectiveness: Based on predictability of the relationship - more predictable relationships provide more persuasive evidence

trend_analysis.description: Comparing current period amounts to prior periods
examples: Compare 2024 sales to 2023, 2022, and 2021 sales
Analyze gross profit percentage trend over 3-5 years
Compare monthly revenue patterns year-over-year
Examine expense categories as percentage of revenue over time
trend_analysis.when_effective: When operations are stable and predictable; less effective during periods of change
trend_analysis.typical_threshold: Investigate variances > 5-10% from prior period or 5-10% above/below expected trend

examples: Current ratio (current assets / current liabilities) - assess if reasonable
Days sales outstanding (A/R / daily sales) - compare to prior year and credit terms
Inventory turnover (COGS / average inventory) - assess for reasonableness
Gross profit percentage (gross profit / sales) - compare to prior periods and industry
Interest coverage ratio (EBIT / interest expense) - verify consistency with debt levels
Asset turnover ratios - assess efficiency of asset utilization
ratio_analysis.when_effective: When stable relationships exist; less effective for fluctuating accounts
ratio_analysis.evaluation: Compare calculated ratios to prior periods, budgets, industry benchmarks, or auditor's expectations

reasonableness_tests.description: Developing independent expectation based on relationships and data
examples: Estimate payroll expense by: # employees × average salary × time period
Estimate interest expense by: average debt balance × weighted average interest rate
Estimate depreciation by: depreciable asset base × average depreciation rate
Estimate rental income by: # units × average rent × occupancy rate × 12 months
Estimate commission expense by: sales × commission percentage
Estimate sales by: units sold × average selling price (from non-financial data)
reasonableness_tests.when_effective: When reliable non-financial data exists to build expectation; very effective for predictable calculations
reasonableness_tests.precision: More precise expectations provide stronger evidence; narrow acceptable range of difference

comparison_to_budgets_forecasts.description: Comparing actual results to management budgets or forecasts
examples: Compare actual revenue to budgeted revenue by product line
Compare actual expenses to budget by department
Analyze variances from forecast and obtain explanations
comparison_to_budgets_forecasts.when_effective: When budgets are realistic and prepared with diligence (not merely aspirational)
limitations: Budgets may not be reliable if management routinely misses targets
Management may manipulate actual results to meet budget
This is client-prepared data, so less independent than auditor-developed expectations
comparison_to_budgets_forecasts.use_with_caution: Corroborate with other evidence; don't rely solely on management's budget

industry_comparisons.description: Comparing client's results to industry averages or competitors
examples: Compare gross profit margin to industry average
Compare SG&A as % of revenue to peer companies
Compare inventory turnover to industry norms
Benchmark financial ratios against similar companies
industry_comparisons.when_effective: When client is comparable to industry averages (similar size, geography, business model)
limitations: Industry data may not be directly comparable (different accounting policies, business models)
Client may legitimately differ from industry average
Industry benchmarks are aggregate data, may not fit specific company
Publicly available industry data may be limited or outdated
industry_comparisons.best_practice: Use as corroborative evidence or to identify areas for investigation, not as primary evidence alone

regression_analysis.description: Statistical technique to model relationship between variables and predict expected values
examples: Predict utility expense based on production volume using historical data
Estimate warranty expense based on sales using regression of past warranty costs to sales
Model relationship between advertising spend and revenue
regression_analysis.when_effective: When strong statistical correlation exists; requires multiple data points (typically several years)
regression_analysis.sophistication: More sophisticated than simple trend or ratio analysis; may require specialist or software
regression_analysis.auditor_skill_required: Must understand regression analysis to properly interpret results and assess reliability

developing_expectations.key_principle: Auditor must develop expectation INDEPENDENTLY before looking at recorded amount
sources_of_information: Anticipated conditions (known changes from prior year)
Non-financial information (production volume, headcount, square footage, etc.)
Relationships between accounts (e.g., sales and cost of sales)
External data (interest rates, commodity prices, economic indicators)

high_precision.description: Expectation is developed with significant accuracy, narrow acceptable range
high_precision.when_achievable: Predictable accounts with stable relationships and reliable data
high_precision.examples: Interest expense (debt × rate), depreciation (assets × rates), rent expense (lease terms)
high_precision.evidence_value: High precision expectations provide more persuasive evidence

moderate_precision.description: Expectation provides general indication of reasonableness, wider acceptable range
moderate_precision.when_used: Somewhat predictable accounts but with some variability
moderate_precision.examples: Revenue by product line, certain operating expenses, gross profit percentages
moderate_precision.evidence_value: Moderate persuasive evidence; may need additional corroboration

low_precision.description: Expectation is very general, very wide acceptable range
low_precision.when_used: Unpredictable accounts or when limited data available for expectation
low_precision.examples: Revenue for new product lines, expenses in volatile categories
low_precision.evidence_value: Limited persuasive evidence; primarily used to identify areas needing detailed testing

required_documentation: Expectation developed and basis for expectation
Data and factors used to develop expectation
Acceptable level of variance (threshold for investigation)
Comparison of recorded amount to expectation
documenting_expectations.timing: Expectation should be documented BEFORE seeing recorded amount to ensure independence

investigating_variances.when_investigation_required: When recorded amount differs from expectation by more than acceptable threshold
investigation_procedures: Inquire of management about reasons for variance
Corroborate explanation with other audit evidence
Consider whether explanation is plausible and consistent with auditor's understanding
Evaluate whether explanation indicates potential misstatement
If explanation is not satisfactory, perform additional tests of details

acceptable_explanations: Known business changes (new product line, facility opened/closed)
Economic factors (price increases, inflation, market changes)
red_flags: Management unable or unwilling to provide support
Pattern of variances in same direction (may indicate bias)
Variances that bring account close to budget or analyst expectations (earnings management)
Complex, convoluted explanations that don't make business sense
evaluating_explanations.when_explanation_unsatisfactory: Perform additional substantive procedures (typically tests of details) to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence

most_effective_for: Large volumes of predictable transactions (payroll, rent, interest)
Accounts with stable relationships to other data (COGS to inventory, interest to debt)
Income statement accounts (easier to predict than balance sheet)
Accounts calculated by formula (depreciation, amortization, interest)
Accounts where expectation can be precisely developed
least_effective_for: Accounts involving significant judgment or estimates (goodwill impairment, loan loss reserves)
Volatile or unpredictable accounts (foreign currency gains/losses)
Accounts susceptible to manipulation or fraud
Accounts where precise expectation cannot be developed
Significant risks (standards require tests of details for significant risks)

cannot_be_used_alone_for.significant_risks: Must perform tests of details; analytical procedures alone are insufficient
cannot_be_used_alone_for.high_fraud_risk_areas: Need direct evidence from tests of details
cannot_be_used_alone_for.complex_estimates: Detailed testing or specialist involvement required

advantages: Efficient - can cover large volumes of transactions quickly
Tests entire population rather than sample
Identifies unusual trends or relationships for further investigation
Provides understanding of business and changes from prior period
Can be performed early in the audit
Useful for directing attention to high-risk areas
limitations: Provides indirect rather than direct evidence
Effectiveness depends on precision of expectation
Less effective for detecting small misstatements that don't affect overall trends
Relies on accuracy of underlying data used to develop expectation
May not detect compensating errors (overstatement offset by understatement)
Cannot substitute for tests of details when direct evidence is needed

tests_of_details.description: Procedures that examine specific items to obtain direct evidence about account balances, transactions, or disclosures

examination_of_documents_and_records.description: Inspecting source documents and accounting records

vouching.definition: Selecting items from accounting records and examining supporting source documents
vouching.direction: From accounting records BACK to source documents
vouching.assertion_tested: Primarily tests EXISTENCE/OCCURRENCE - did the recorded transaction actually occur?
vouching.example: Select sales transactions from sales journal and examine shipping documents, sales orders, and customer invoices to verify the sales actually occurred
vouching.when_used: When risk of overstatement (fictitious transactions, premature revenue recognition)

tracing.definition: Selecting source documents and following them forward into accounting records
tracing.direction: From source documents FORWARD to accounting records
tracing.assertion_tested: Primarily tests COMPLETENESS - were all transactions recorded?
tracing.example: Select shipping documents and trace forward to sales invoices and sales journal to verify all shipments were recorded as sales
tracing.when_used: When risk of understatement (unrecorded transactions, cutoff issues)

inspection.definition: Examining documents for information or evidence of authorization, accuracy, authenticity
examples: Inspect vendor invoices for proper authorization and agreement to purchase order
Inspect contracts for terms affecting revenue recognition
Inspect bank statements for unusual transactions
Inspect loan agreements for debt covenant requirements
Examine board minutes for significant transactions approved
inspection.assertions_tested: Varies - can test existence, rights, accuracy, presentation depending on document

examination_of_documents_and_records.sample_vs_population: Usually performed on sample basis; sample size depends on risk assessment and desired detection risk

external_confirmations.description: Obtaining direct communication from third party regarding information in financial statements

positive_confirmation.description: Recipient asked to respond whether they agree or disagree with information
positive_confirmation.when_used: Higher risk situations; when response is critical
positive_confirmation.response_rate: Typically 40-70% initial response rate; follow-up required for non-responses

forms.blank_confirmation: Does not provide amount; recipient fills in their records (more reliable but lower response rate)
forms.invoice_confirmation: Provides amount; recipient confirms or notes exceptions (higher response rate)

negative_confirmation.description: Recipient asked to respond ONLY if they disagree with information
negative_confirmation.when_used: Lower risk situations, large number of small balances, low assessed risk of material misstatement, reasonable to expect recipients will give consideration
negative_confirmation.limitation: Lack of response does not provide explicit evidence; recipient may not have reviewed
negative_confirmation.not_sufficient_alone: If using negative confirmations, must also perform other substantive procedures

accounts_receivable.purpose: Confirm existence and gross amount of receivables
accounts_receivable.does_not_test: Valuation/collectability (customer may owe money but be unable to pay)

accounts_payable.purpose: Confirm completeness and amount of payables, especially when risk of understatement
accounts_payable.typical_approach: Confirm with vendors from whom significant purchases made, including zero-balance vendors
accounts_payable.why_zero_balances: Unrecorded liability may exist with vendor not showing balance in client's records

bank_balances.purpose: Confirm cash balances, loans, and other arrangements with financial institutions
bank_balances.standard_form: Standard Bank Confirmation (requires management to authorize bank to respond)
bank_balances.information_confirmed: Deposit accounts, loan balances, collateral pledges, lines of credit, contingent liabilities

investments.purpose: Confirm holdings with broker or custodian
investments.information_confirmed: Number of shares/bonds, description, cost basis, market value

legal_matters.purpose: Confirm litigation, claims, assessments with client's attorneys
legal_matters.information_sought: Pending or threatened litigation, claims, assessments; attorney's evaluation of likelihood and amount
legal_matters.limitations: Attorney may limit response to matters where they provided legal services; may not evaluate likelihood
legal_matters.assertions: Completeness of contingencies, valuation of contingent liabilities, disclosure adequacy

debt.purpose: Confirm loan balances, terms, interest rates, collateral, covenants
debt.information_confirmed: Principal balance, interest rate, payment terms, maturity, collateral pledged, covenant requirements
debt.assertions: Existence, completeness, accuracy, rights and obligations, presentation (current vs. long-term)

steps: Determine information to be confirmed and appropriate third parties
Select sample of accounts/items to confirm
Prepare confirmation requests (auditor controls; client signs authorization)
Auditor mails confirmations (maintains control over confirmation process)
Receive responses directly from third parties (sent to auditor, not client)
confirmation_process.auditor_control_critical: Auditor must maintain control over confirmation process - select items, prepare confirmations, mail them, receive responses directly. Client involvement limited to authorization only.

handling_responses.agreements: Agree confirmed amount to client's records; investigate any differences
handling_responses.exceptions: Investigate cause - may be timing differences, errors, or misstatements
handling_responses.non_responses: Perform alternative procedures (examine subsequent cash receipts, shipping documents, invoices, etc.)
alternative_procedures_for_receivables: Examine subsequent cash collection from customer
Examine supporting documentation (sales orders, shipping documents, invoices)
handling_responses.second_requests: Send second request if no response to first request
handling_responses.insufficient_responses: If response rate too low, increase sample size or perform more extensive alternative procedures

limitations: Only addresses assertions confirmed - e.g., A/R confirmation doesn't test collectability
Depends on third party's competence and willingness to respond accurately
Non-responses require alternative procedures (less reliable evidence)
Subject to interception or manipulation if auditor doesn't control process
May not detect all errors (e.g., timing differences in A/P)

physical_inspection.description: Auditor's direct observation or examination of tangible assets

inventory_observation.requirement: When inventory is material, auditor generally required to attend physical inventory count (AU-C 501)
inventory_observation.timing: At or near year-end (if counted at interim, also test rollforward procedures)
procedures: Test count accuracy by selecting items and recounting
Record test counts in working papers for later tracing to final inventory compilation
Observe condition of inventory (damaged, obsolete, slow-moving)
Assess adequacy of cutoff procedures (last items received, shipped)
Observe segregation of inventory (client's vs. consigned, held for others)
inventory_observation.assertions_tested: Existence (primarily), completeness (observation of procedures), condition (affects valuation)
inventory_observation.does_not_test: Ownership (rights), valuation/pricing, completeness of items not at locations visited
inventory_observation.if_cannot_attend: May need to disclaim opinion or qualify opinion due to scope limitation

cash_count.when_performed: If client has significant cash on hand (petty cash, retail operations)
cash_count.procedures: Count cash in presence of custodian, obtain acknowledgment of return of cash
cash_count.timing: Surprise counts preferred to prevent substitution

fixed_assets_inspection.procedures: Physically observe and inspect significant fixed assets
fixed_assets_inspection.when_performed: For material additions, when fraud risk exists, or when physical condition affects valuation
fixed_assets_inspection.scope: Typically test sample, not all assets, unless red flags exist

securities_inspection.procedures: Inspect securities certificates if held by client
securities_inspection.timing: Simultaneous count of all negotiable assets to prevent substitution
securities_inspection.note: Most securities now held electronically - confirmation with custodian more common

physical_inspection.effectiveness: Provides strong evidence of existence and condition; does not address rights, valuation, or completeness

recalculation.definition: Checking mathematical accuracy of documents or records
examples: Recalculate depreciation expense
Recalculate interest expense or accrued interest
Foot (add down) and cross-foot (add across) schedules
Verify mathematical accuracy of invoices
Recalculate commission expenses
Verify accuracy of inventory extensions (quantity × price)
recalculation.reliability: High reliability for calculation accuracy; does not address underlying data accuracy

reperformance.definition: Independent execution of procedures or controls
examples: Reperform bank reconciliation independently
Reperform aging of accounts receivable
Reperform inventory rollforward from count date to year-end
Reperform reconciliation of sub-ledger to general ledger
reperformance.assertions_tested: Varies by procedure - typically accuracy, completeness

analytical_procedures_as_substantive_tes.note: Though analytical procedures are a type of substantive procedure, they're distinguished from tests of details
analytical_procedures_as_substantive_tes.relationship: Often used in combination - analytics to identify areas for detailed testing; tests of details to investigate variances

designing_tests_of_details.assertion_driven: Tests must be designed to address specific assertions for specific accounts

existence_occurrence: Vouch recorded transactions to supporting documents
completeness: Trace source documents to accounting records
Perform analytical procedures to identify missing transactions
Review subsequent periods for items that should have been recorded in current period
accuracy_valuation: Test pricing (agree to vendor invoices, price lists)
rights_and_obligations: Confirm with third parties (especially for assets held by others)
Review financing agreements for asset pledges
Confirm absence of liens or encumbrances
presentation_and_disclosure: Read financial statements and compare to GAAP requirements
Review footnote disclosures for completeness and accuracy
Verify classification (current vs. noncurrent, operating vs. financing, etc.)
Confirm related party transactions are disclosed

factors_increasing_sample_size: Higher assessed risk of material misstatement (IR and CR)
Less reliable audit evidence from other procedures
factors_decreasing_sample_size: Lower assessed risk of material misstatement

combining_substantive_procedures.balanced_approach: Auditors typically use combination of substantive analytical procedures AND tests of details

revenue: Analytical: Compare revenue by month to prior year, analyze revenue per customer/product, calculate and analyze gross margin trends
Tests of details: Vouch sample of sales transactions to shipping documents and customer orders, test cutoff, confirm accounts receivable
accounts_receivable: Analytical: Calculate and analyze days sales outstanding, aging analysis compared to prior periods and credit terms
Tests of details: Confirm balances with customers, examine subsequent cash collections, evaluate allowance for doubtful accounts
inventory: Analytical: Calculate and analyze inventory turnover and gross profit percentages
Tests of details: Observe physical count, test pricing, test lower-of-cost-or-market, evaluate obsolescence reserves
fixed_assets: Analytical: Analyze depreciation expense as percentage of asset base, compare to prior years
Tests of details: Vouch additions to invoices and supporting documents, inspect major acquisitions, recalculate depreciation for sample of assets
accounts_payable: Analytical: Calculate days payable outstanding, compare to prior periods and payment terms
Tests of details: Confirm with vendors (especially zero balances), search for unrecorded liabilities, test cutoff
payroll: Analytical: Estimate total payroll by # employees × average salary, analyze by department
Tests of details: Test sample of payroll transactions for proper authorization and accuracy, reconcile quarterly tax returns to payroll records
debt: Analytical: Recalculate interest expense based on debt balances and rates, compare to actual
Tests of details: Confirm debt balances and terms with lenders, examine debt agreements, verify compliance with covenants

when_to_emphasize_tests_of_details: Accounts involving complex estimates or significant judgment
When analytical procedures cannot achieve desired precision
First year audits (limited comparability to prior years)
when_analytics_may_be_primary_procedure: When precise expectation can be developed
Income statement accounts (more predictable than balance sheet)

year_end_testing.description: Procedures performed at or very close to balance sheet date
advantages: Addresses account balances as of balance sheet date directly
Lower detection risk - less time for changes after testing
Required for cash confirmations, inventory observations
disadvantages: Less time to investigate and resolve issues before deadline
when_required: Accounts susceptible to manipulation near period-end
When interim testing not feasible or efficient

interim_testing.description: Procedures performed during the year before balance sheet date
advantages: Spreads work over longer period - less time pressure
Issues can be identified and resolved earlier
More efficient use of audit resources
disadvantages: Requires rollforward procedures from interim to year-end
Creates gap period risk - misstatements could occur after testing
May require duplicate work if issues arise at year-end
when_appropriate: Strong internal controls that are tested and effective
Accounts with low risk of manipulation at year-end
When efficient rollforward procedures can be performed

typical_procedures: Perform substantive analytical procedures on activity from interim to year-end
Test significant unusual transactions in gap period
Update risk assessment based on changes in gap period
Consider whether gap period results are consistent with expectations
Perform targeted tests of details for high-risk transactions in gap period
rollforward_procedures.consideration: If significant unexpected changes in gap period, may need more extensive year-end procedures

extent_of_substantive_testing.relationship_to_detection_risk: Lower required detection risk → More extensive substantive testing needed

risk_assessment: Significant risk designation → Extensive testing required
materiality: Account is larger percentage of materiality → More testing
evidence_from_other_procedures: Effective analytical procedures → Less detailed testing may be acceptable
Strong controls tested → Can reduce substantive testing extent
population_characteristics: More variability in population → Larger samples needed
Larger account balances → More items tested

for_analytical_procedures: Level of disaggregation (total company vs. by division/product/month)

sufficiency_evaluation.question: Have we obtained sufficient appropriate evidence to reduce audit risk to acceptably low level?
considerations: Consistency of evidence from different sources
Whether sufficient evidence for significant risks
Professional judgment about whether evidence is persuasive
sufficiency_evaluation.if_insufficient: Perform additional procedures or modify opinion if scope limitation

key_concepts: Substantive procedures are REQUIRED for all material accounts regardless of control effectiveness
Two types: substantive analytical procedures and tests of details
Significant risks require tests of details - cannot rely solely on analytics
Vouching tests existence (from records to documents), tracing tests completeness (from documents to records)
Confirmations must be controlled by auditor for reliability
Lower detection risk requires more extensive substantive testing
Analytical procedures are most effective for predictable accounts with stable relationships
common_exam_questions: Which substantive procedure tests which assertion?
When are tests of details required vs. when can analytics be used?
What's the difference between vouching and tracing?
When would auditor increase extent of substantive procedures?
What are appropriate responses to analytical procedure variances?

memorization_aids.vouching_vs_tracing: Vouching = V = Verify existence (recorded items really exist). Tracing = T = Test completeness (all items are recorded)
memorization_aids.confirmation_control: Auditor must CONTROL: selection, preparation, mailing, receiving responses
memorization_aids.significant_risks: Significant = need Specific procedures = tests of details required

summary: Substantive procedures are the heart of the audit, providing direct evidence about whether financial statements are materially misstated. Required for all material accounts regardless of control strength, substantive procedures come in two forms: substantive analytical procedures (indirect evidence through relationships and comparisons) and tests of details (direct examination of transactions and balances). The choice and extent depend on risk assessment - higher risks demand more extensive tests of details, while lower risks may allow greater reliance on analytics. Understanding when each type is appropriate, how to design procedures responsive to specific assertions, and how to evaluate the sufficiency of evidence obtained is essential for CPA AUD success. Key principle: analytical procedures are efficient but indirect; tests of details are time-consuming but provide direct evidence. Most audits use a balanced combination of both.
references: AU-C Section 330 - Performing Audit Procedures in Response to Assessed Risks
AU-C Section 501 - Audit Evidence—Specific Considerations for Selected Items
PCAOB AS 2301 - The Auditor's Responses to the Risks of Material Misstatement
